intro: “The Alcotts” is the third movement of Ives’s Piano Sonata No. 2, “Concord, Mass., 1840–60”. Ives took the music heard at the Alcotts’ piano, hymns and Scottish songs along with Beethoven’s Fifth, and made from it the broad C major melody at the centre of the Concord Sonata.

sections.label: A · Hymn melody in two keys
sections.mNote: A B♭ melody sounds above A♭ bass chords.

sections.label: A′ · Fifth Symphony motto among dissonant chords
sections.mNote: Repeated notes from the Fifth Symphony are heard at the climaxes.

sections.label: B · Scottish songs at the piano
sections.mNote: A parlour tune twice comes close to Wagner’s wedding music

sections.label: Link · Parlour tune with chromatic inflection
sections.mNote: Chromatic notes are added to the song-like phrases.

sections.label: A″ · The whole tune in C major
sections.mNote: Broad piano chords join the earlier fragments into one tune.

sections.label: Coda · B♭ recalled, close in C major
sections.mNote: B♭ returns briefly; the last chord is in C major.

relations.label: The parlour melody returns
relations.basis: The paired spans lie in the middle parlour-music episode, whose melodic paragraph recurs. Kyle Gann describes its two turns towards Wagner’s wedding tune at https://charlesives.org/node/6616; this link concerns the longer paragraph, not an individually timed quotation. CENS diagonal mean 0.940, sustained 29 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 40.5 s (cache/form/ives-concord-alcotts.txt, candidate 1; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

cues.title: Hymn melody in B♭ over A♭
cues.text: The piano plays a hymn-like melody in B♭ over bass chords in A♭. The tune is close to complete here. Fragments of this melody appear throughout the Concord Sonata.
cues.evidence: Kyle Gann, “Following the Concord Sonata”, section “The Alcotts”: opening human-faith melody in B♭ with A♭ bass chords. https://charlesives.org/node/6616
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Ives on the Orchard House spinet, 1920
cues.text: In his 1920 essay, Ives pointed to a “little old spinet-piano” at Orchard House. His account combined the Alcott family with Little Women. In it, Beth played Scottish airs and tried her hand at Beethoven’s Fifth.
cues.evidence: Charles Ives, Essays Before a Sonata (1920), “The Alcotts”, paragraph beginning “Concord village”: the spinet and Beth’s playing. https://www.gutenberg.org/files/3673/3673-h/3673-h.htm#alcotts

cues.title: Beethoven’s Fifth and Missionary Hymn
cues.text: The short-short-short-long figure of Beethoven’s Fifth sounds through the piano chords. A second borrowed tune, Missionary Hymn, enters, and its repeated notes also fall by a third. Ives sets the two against each other in different keys.
cues.evidence: Gann, “The Alcotts”: the relationship between Missionary Hymn and the Beethoven figure, and the dissonant climaxes. https://charlesives.org/node/6616
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Middle episode, parlour music
cues.text: The middle episode is a song-like piano passage in the manner of parlour music. Its turns follow the idiom of Scottish folk song, and twice it quotes the wedding march from Wagner’s Lohengrin.
cues.evidence: Gann, “The Alcotts”: the middle parlour-music episode, Scottish-song idiom and two references to the wedding march from Lohengrin. https://charlesives.org/node/6616
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Public première, Town Hall, 1939
cues.text: On 20 January 1939 John Kirkpatrick gave the complete sonata its public première at New York’s Town Hall. He had already played it from memory at a private concert in Cos Cob on 28 November 1938. By then the score had been in circulation for eighteen years.
cues.evidence: Gann’s chronology: circulation in January 1921, private complete performance at Cos Cob on 28 November 1938, and public première on 20 January 1939. https://charlesives.org/node/6616

cues.title: Chromatic transition
cues.text: The Scottish-song turns are extended into a chromatic passage. Piano chords cluster around the melody and lead to a much broader statement of the sonata’s recurring tune.
cues.evidence: Gann, “The Alcotts”: the chromatic transition transforms the Scottish-song idiom before the final C major statement. https://charlesives.org/node/6616
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Full melody in C major
cues.text: The whole melody is played in broad C major chords, with both hands. Its rising do–re–mi and Beethoven’s repeated-note figure now form one continuous tune.
cues.evidence: Gann’s Example 1 and “The Alcotts” identify the complete human-faith melody, its opening scale and Beethoven component, and its final C major setting. https://charlesives.org/node/6616
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Final C major cadence
cues.text: Near the end the music briefly returns to B♭. The piano then closes on a C major chord.
cues.evidence: Gann, “The Alcotts”, final paragraph: B♭ briefly recalled before the last C major chord. https://charlesives.org/node/6616
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Quiet restatement, then the parlour episode
transitions.from: A′ · Fifth Symphony motto among dissonant chords
transitions.to: B · Scottish songs at the piano
transitions.how: After the Beethoven climax, the recurring melody returns at a quiet level over dissonant piano chords. In the next episode, the parlour episode, a song-like upper line is set apart from its accompaniment. Scottish turns and a brief allusion to Wagner’s wedding music replace the pounding repeated notes.
transitions.evidence: Gann, “The Alcotts”: quiet restatement following the climax, then the parlour episode. https://charlesives.org/node/6616

transitions.title: Parlour tune leads to C major melody
transitions.from: B · Scottish songs at the piano
transitions.to: Link · Parlour tune with chromatic inflection
transitions.how: The piano keeps the Scottish turns of the parlour tune and alters them with chromatic notes. The chords grow more crowded and the plain accompaniment is disturbed. The harmony becomes ambiguous. The song idiom changes gradually, and this passage forms the link to the broad C major melody.
transitions.evidence: Gann, “The Alcotts”: the harmonically ambiguous transition gradually transforms the Scottish-song idiom. https://charlesives.org/node/6616

transitions.title: Chromatic passage into C major melody
transitions.from: Link · Parlour tune with chromatic inflection
transitions.to: A″ · The whole tune in C major
transitions.how: The chromatic piano passage moves into the complete recurring melody in C major. Both hands play broad chords beneath its do–re–mi opening and the repeated notes taken from Beethoven. The fragments heard in the earlier movements are joined here in a single phrase.
transitions.evidence: Gann, Example 1 and “The Alcotts”: the complete C major statement and its component phrases. https://charlesives.org/node/6616

transitions.title: B♭ before the final C major chord
transitions.from: A″ · The whole tune in C major
transitions.to: Coda · B♭ recalled, close in C major
transitions.how: The broad C major chords grow quieter as the theme dies away. B♭, the key of the opening, returns briefly before the closing C major chord. The last change of harmony falls within the slowing piano phrase.
transitions.evidence: Gann, “The Alcotts”, final paragraph: the dying-away theme, momentary B♭ and final C major chord. https://charlesives.org/node/6616

composer.epithet: Composer and New York life-insurance salesman whose music sets a hymn heard across a river against a marching band.
facts: His father George Ives; Horatio Parker at Yale, 1894–98
Church organist until 1902; insurance executive at Ives & Myrick
Concord Sonata and Essays Before a Sonata, 1920; 114 Songs, 1922
Danbury bands and hymn singing; the New England of Emerson and Thoreau
composer.background:
George Ives played his cornet across a pond so that his son could hear what distance did to the sound. He made the boy sing in one key while he accompanied in another, built instruments that could play quarter-tones and tried out the collision of two marching bands. A former Union Army bandmaster, he earned his living teaching and directing music in Danbury, Connecticut, where his son Charles was born in 1874.

The lessons also involved work. By fourteen Charles was a salaried church organist; at seventeen he wrote the Variations on America, a set of variations for keyboard on the tune of God Save the King. At Yale, which he entered in 1894, Horatio Parker taught him counterpoint, orchestration and the construction of a symphony. His First Symphony, written in a European idiom, came out of that teaching. George died of a stroke during Charles’s first term.
